Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

| Requirement | Status |
|---|---|
| `fn describe_error(err: &(dyn std::error::Error + 'static)) -> String`, module-private, above `row_to_domain_event` | Met — exact signature and placement (`relay.rs:64`). |

| Test: sourceless error → its own `Display` | Met verbatim (`describe_error_of_a_sourceless_error_is_just_its_display`). |
| Call site: `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` → `.map_err(|e| describe_error(&e))` at `relay.rs:124`(orig) | Met exactly (`relay.rs:143` post-diff). |
| `PublishError` in `ports.rs` untouched | Met — confirmed via `git diff eb6c690..7680a2f -- .../ports.rs` = empty. |

| Commit: conventional, workspace scope, lowercase subject, ≤100 chars, no body/no `#NNN` | Met — `fix(rs): render the full publish-error source chain in relay reasons (SMA-469)`, 78 chars, no body. |
| Only `relay.rs` in the commit | Met — diff stat shows exactly 1 file. |

No YAGNI/scope-creep: the implementation is a near-literal transcription of the brief's suggested code, nothing extra added.

**The reported deviation, judged on its merits:** the brief said to add `PublishError` to the plain top-level import; the implementer instead used `#[cfg(test)] use paigasus_iam_core::PublishError;`. I verified independently:
- `rs/Cargo.toml` sets `[workspace.lints.rust] warnings = "deny"`; `paigasus-iam`'s `Cargo.toml` has `[lints] workspace = true`.
- `paigasus-iam` has both a `[lib]` and a `[[bin]]` target, and grepping the whole file, `PublishError` is referenced only inside `mod tests` (the `map_err` call site never names the type — it's inferred).
- An unconditional import would therefore be a genuinely unused import in the non-test (lib/bin) compilation, which `deny(warnings)` turns into a hard build error.

The fix is **correct** (it compiles in both modes: elided entirely outside `cfg(test)`, present and used inside it) and **minimal** (one attribute added, no restructuring). It's not quite the *cleanest* possible form — putting `use paigasus_iam_core::PublishError;` directly inside the `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block (which is already fully gated) would achieve the identical effect with better locality, keeping test-only imports out of the production-import block at file top. That's a legitimate, arguable style nit, not a defect — flagging as **Minor/contestable** below.

## B. Task quality — Approved

**Correctness**
- `describe_error`'s loop terminates correctly for the chain shapes this codebase can actually produce: `PublishError::Backend` wraps a `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` whose `source()` eventually returns `None` for any well-behaved (thiserror-derived or std) error type. There is no cycle guard, but reachability of a self-referential `source()` chain here would require a pathologically-implemented `Error` in a dependency — not something this task needs to defend against, and not something `anyhow`/std itself guards against either. **Minor, theoretical, not reachable.**
- Call site `.map_err(|e| describe_error(&e))`: `e: PublishError` (from `publisher.publish`'s `Result<(), PublishError>`), and `&e` unsize-coerces to `&dyn std::error::Error + 'static` because the target type is known from `describe_error`'s signature — no explicit cast needed, and PublishError doesn't need to be in scope by name for this coercion. Confirmed correct by the report's clean `cargo clippy -D warnings` + full-suite pass.

**Test quality**
- The primary test (`..._without_duplicating_levels`) is a real behavioral assertion, not a rubber-stamp: `PublishError::Backend`'s own `Display` is the static `"backend error"`, so a trivial `describe_error(err) = err.to_string()` implementation would produce `"backend error"`, not the expected `"backend error: publish failed: transport closed"` — the test would fail against that naive implementation. Good.
- The second test (sourceless → own `Display`) would pass against a trivial `to_string()`-only implementation too, but it's clearly meant to pair with the first, not stand alone as the chain-walk proof — appropriate as a boundary-condition check.

**Doc comments**: accurate and specific about *why* — calls out that `Display` is static, that `#[from]` routes the cause to `source()` not the message, and connects the chain walk to concrete downstream consumers (`last_error`, `error!`/`warn!`). No overclaiming.

**Issues found**

- **Minor / contestable** — `#[cfg(test)] use paigasus_iam_core::PublishError;` sits at file-top among production imports rather than inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` where it's used. Functionally identical either way; the in-module placement is arguably more idiomatic/conventional Rust and keeps the top-level import block production-only. Not a defect, just a style preference — reasonable people could land on either side.
- **Minor / theoretical** — `describe_error`'s `while let Some(e) = source` has no cycle guard against a self-referential `source()` chain. Not reachable with the error types in play here (thiserror-derived, single-field `#[source]`), and adding protection wasn't requested by the brief. Flagging only for completeness.

No Critical or Important issues found.

That second assertion is the one that actually distinguishes `now()` from `occurred_at`; a bare `IS NOT NULL` check would pass under either. (`start_raw_postgres` is private to `audit_log_partition_pg.rs` — each test binary compiles its own `mod support;` — so it needs promoting to `support/mod.rs` or copying, matching the existing duplication posture in that file.)

- **Minor:** the index assertions check names only, not `pg_indexes.indexdef`. `CREATE INDEX ix_event_outbox_published ON event_outbox (id)` with no predicate would pass. Asserting the `indexdef` substring (`(published_at)` / `WHERE (published_at IS NOT NULL)`) costs one line each.
- **Minor:** no assertion on column type or nullability. `parked_at TEXT` would pass.

### 6. Entity doc comments vs. actual behavior — **Minor, but three separate problems**

```rust
/// When the relay flipped `parked` to true (SMA-469). `[outbox.retention].parked_days`
/// measures from this, never from `occurred_at`. NULL only for a row that is not parked.
```
a. **Forward-dated.** `relay.rs:157` today does `active.parked = Set(true)` and nothing else — the relay does *not* set `parked_at`, and `[outbox.retention]` does not exist. Both arrive in Tasks 3/5. Within a plan that lands as one PR this is a non-issue; as committed-at-this-SHA prose it describes code that isn't there.

b. **"NULL only for a row that is not parked" states an invariant nothing enforces.** No CHECK constraint, and the current relay violates it for any row parked between m0009 and the Task-3 deploy. (Both sides: adding `CHECK (parked = false OR parked_at IS NOT NULL)` would be *wrong* here — during a rolling deploy an old replica parking a row without `parked_at` would then hard-fail. Not adding it is the right call; the doc should say "expected to be non-NULL for parked rows, not enforced by the schema.")

c. **`last_error`'s doc is self-contradictory.** "rewritten on EVERY failed attempt … so an operator watching `attempts` climb sees the current cause" and "Deliberately preserved across a replay, so a re-parked row keeps the original evidence" cannot both hold — if it's rewritten on every attempt, a re-parked row keeps the *latest* error, not the original. The intended meaning is presumably "replay does not NULL it out," which is worth saying in those words.

### 7. Minor — module-doc precision on the concurrency rationale

The doc states a bare `ADD COLUMN` "would fail the losing replica of a simultaneous first boot with `column "parked_at" ... already exists`." With sea-orm-migration 1.1.20 the *entire* `Migrator::up` run is wrapped in one Postgres transaction (`exec_with_connection`, migrator.rs:263), so the losing replica's DDL blocks on the winner's lock and then rolls back cleanly — and would fail anyway on `seaql_migrations`' version PK. The idempotent-DDL convention is still correct (re-run safety, defense in depth, repo consistency, and the constraint you set), but the specific failure mode narrated here is not quite the one that occurs. Worth one sentence of correction rather than a rewrite.

### 8. Nit

`audit_log_partition_pg.rs:208` — `Migrator::up(&db, None).await.expect("m0008 must apply correctly under a non-UTC session TZ")` now applies m0008 **and** m0009 under `TimeZone='America/New_York'`. Harmless (`now()` on a `timestamptz` is TZ-independent), but the message is now inaccurate.

---

| # | Severity | Issue |
|---|---|---|
| 5a | **Important** | The `parked_at = now()` backfill — the task's single most consequential guarantee — has zero test coverage, and the test's module doc falsely claims it is covered |
| 2 | **Important** | `Migrator::down(&db, Some(2))` is correct today but is a hard-coded step count that must be bumped by every future migration; a robust in-file alternative (`start_raw_postgres` + `up(Some(8))` + `down(Some(1))`) exists |
| 5b/5c | Minor | Index assertions check names not `indexdef`; no column type/nullability assertion |
| 6a/6b/6c | Minor | Entity docs describe unimplemented behavior, assert an unenforced invariant, and contain a self-contradiction on `last_error` |
| 3 | Minor | `ix_event_outbox_parked ON (id)` doesn't serve the parked-retention `parked_at < cutoff` sweep — fine at DLQ scale, but Task 6 shouldn't assume otherwise |
| 7 | Minor | Module doc's concurrent-boot failure mode is imprecise given SeaORM's single-transaction migration run |
| 8 | Nit | Stale `expect` message at `audit_log_partition_pg.rs:208` |

Nothing is Critical: the migration SQL, the backfill source, the idempotency, the `lock_timeout`, the `down()`, and the model-literal fallout are all correct. ⚠️ Cannot verify from diff: test execution results (per instructions, taken from the report — which credibly documents a clean 546/546 at `--test-threads=4` plus isolated re-runs of the two contention flakes).

Task 2 review came back: spec ✅, but task quality needs work. Two **Important** findings to fix. Fix round 1 of 5.

You are still in the worktree — confirm `git branch --show-current` is the SMA-469 feature branch before touching anything.

---

**Finding 1 (Important) — the backfill has zero test coverage, and the test's module doc falsely claims otherwise.**

`tests/outbox_dead_letter_columns_pg.rs`'s module doc says "…and every row already parked at migration time is backfilled with a non-NULL `parked_at`." The test body never checks this. So the single most consequential correctness property in the whole task — `parked_at = now()` rather than `occurred_at` — has no coverage at all. A future edit changing `now()` to `occurred_at` would pass the suite, and the resulting bug (every pre-existing parked row instantly eligible for deletion by a retention window it predates) is silent and unrecoverable.

This gap came from the brief, not from you — the brief's own Step 1 code and doc have the same mismatch. Fix it anyway.

Add a test that actually distinguishes the two. Shape:

1. `start_raw_postgres()` (NOT `start_migrated_postgres`), then `Migrator::up(&db, Some(8))` to pin the DB to m0001..m0008 — i.e. before m0009 exists.
2. Raw-`INSERT` an `event_outbox` row with `parked = true` and `occurred_at = now() - interval '90 days'`.
3. `Migrator::up(&db, None)` to apply m0009.
4. Assert `parked_at IS NOT NULL` **and** `parked_at > occurred_at + interval '80 days'`.

That second assertion is the one that matters — a bare `IS NOT NULL` check passes under either `now()` or `occurred_at`, so it would not catch the bug.

Note `start_raw_postgres()` is currently private to `tests/audit_log_partition_pg.rs`, and each test binary compiles its own `mod support;`. Either promote it into `tests/support/mod.rs` (preferred — a later task in this plan needs the same helper) or copy it, matching that file's existing posture. If you promote it, make sure you do not break `audit_log_partition_pg.rs`.

While you are in that file, correct the module doc so it describes exactly what the tests now assert.

---

**Finding 2 (Important) — `Migrator::down(&db, Some(2))` is correct today but is a latent trap.**

Your diagnosis and causality proof were right, and `Some(2)` does preserve the test's original meaning. The problem is the formulation: the step count is now coupled to "how many migrations exist after m0008." Tasks 3-19 of this plan, and every future migration, must remember to bump it — and when someone forgets, the failure surfaces as an assertion failure in an unrelated `audit_log` test whose message points at m0008. It also silently couples that test to m0009's `down` succeeding.

Replace it with a formulation that pins the DB by construction instead of counting backwards. The same file already uses this pattern in two other tests:

```rust

Migrator::up(&db, Some(8)).await.expect("m0001..m0008 must apply");
// ... seed ...
Migrator::down(&db, Some(1)).await.expect("m0008 down must succeed");
```

Now "one step back" IS m0008, permanently, regardless of what lands on top. Adapt it to whatever that test actually does — read the whole test first and preserve its every assertion. Restore the `expect` messages to accurately name what they cover.

Also fix the now-inaccurate `expect` message at roughly `audit_log_partition_pg.rs:208` — `Migrator::up(&db, None)` there applies m0008 **and** m0009 under the non-UTC session TZ, but the message names only m0008.

---

**When done:** re-run the tests covering the amended code — at minimum:

```bash

cd rs && cargo nextest run -p paigasus-iam --test outbox_dead_letter_columns_pg --test audit_log_partition_pg --test-threads=4
```

`char_indices()` yields cumulative byte offsets that are always char-start boundaries, strictly increasing (every char ≥1 byte). `take_while(|i| *i <= MAX_ERROR_BYTES).last()` therefore always yields either `0` or some `char_indices`-produced offset that is `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES` — so `s[..end]` is always a valid slice (never mid-character) and always `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES` bytes. `unwrap_or(0)` is genuinely unreachable (offset `0` always satisfies the predicate). Edge cases:
- `s.len() == MAX_ERROR_BYTES` exactly → early return, unchanged, no ellipsis. Correct.
- First char alone `> MAX_ERROR_BYTES` (hypothetically, if the bound were tiny) → `end = 0`, output is just `"…"`. No panic, correctly bounded.
Bound is genuinely guaranteed: `s[..end].len() == end <= MAX_ERROR_BYTES`, so total output `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES + '…'.len_utf8()`.

## Verdict B — Task quality: Needs work (one Important finding; contestable — see below)

**B.1 `truncate_error` cannot panic and cannot exceed its bound — TRUE, proven.**
`char_indices()` yields cumulative byte offsets that are always char-start boundaries, strictly increasing (every char ≥1 byte). `take_while(|i| *i <= MAX_ERROR_BYTES).last()` therefore always yields either `0` or some `char_indices`-produced offset that is `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES` — so `s[..end]` is always a valid slice (never mid-character) and always `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES` bytes. `unwrap_or(0)` is genuinely unreachable (offset `0` always satisfies the predicate). Edge cases:
- `s.len() == MAX_ERROR_BYTES` exactly → early return, unchanged, no ellipsis. Correct.
- First char alone `> MAX_ERROR_BYTES` (hypothetically, if the bound were tiny) → `end = 0`, output is just `"…"`. No panic, correctly bounded.
Bound is genuinely guaranteed: `s[..end].len() == end <= MAX_ERROR_BYTES`, so total output `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES + '…'.len_utf8()`.

**B.2 Important — the multi-byte truncation test does not test what its comment claims.**
`"😀".repeat(700)` uses a uniform 4-byte character, and `MAX_ERROR_BYTES = 1024` is an exact multiple of 4 (`1024 = 4×256`). Byte offset 1024 is *always* a valid char boundary for this string, regardless of implementation. Working the numbers: `end` computed by the real implementation is exactly `1024` (chars 0–255), and a naive `&s[..MAX_ERROR_BYTES]` slice is *identical* — same 1024-byte prefix, no panic, byte-for-byte the same output. Every assertion in the test (`len <=`, `ends_with('…')`, `chars().all(|c| c == '😀')`) passes equally for both.

- The test's own inline comment — *"a naive byte slice would have panicked before we got here"* — is not actually demonstrated for this data; it's an unearned assertion.
- A test that would actually discriminate needs the cut point to land mid-character, e.g. a character whose width does not evenly divide 1024 (a 3-byte char: `1024 mod 3 = 1`), or a leading non-4-byte-aligned prefix before the repeated emoji.
- Note on attribution: this exact snippet is the brief's Step 1 code, transcribed verbatim (confirmed byte-for-byte against the diff) — the implementer didn't invent the weak test, but it is what shipped in this task's commit.
- Countervailing point (why this could be judged Minor instead): the *implementation* is independently proven correct by the general argument in B.1, which does not depend on this specific test. The gap is in regression protection, not in current correctness. Reasonable reviewers could rate this Minor for that reason; I rate it Important because this exact "does the char-boundary test actually test the panic case" question is precisely what the review brief asked to verify, and the answer is no.

**B.3 Relay failure branch — correct.** `outcome` merges `row_to_domain_event`'s malformed-row `Err` and `publisher.publish`'s `Err` into one `Err(reason)` match arm; `last_error` is set unconditionally in that arm (covers both failure sources). `parked_at` is set only inside the `attempts >= self.max_attempts` block, in the same branch as `parked = true`. Both ride the single `active.update(&txn)` call after the match — one statement, same `txn` opened at the top of `tick` via `self.db.begin()`. All GLOBAL CONSTRAINTS on this point are satisfied.

**B.4 Integration assertion — genuinely proves the chain walk and the timestamp.** `PublishError::Backend`'s `Display` is the static `"backend error"` (thiserror `#[error("backend error")]`); `FailingPublisher` produces a boxed string-error source `"always fails"` with no further source. So the assertions do prove `describe_error`'s chain walk survived into storage. `row.parked_at.is_some()` directly proves the timestamp was stamped. The added `else`-branch assertions (`last_error.is_some()`, `parked_at.is_none()` on non-parking failures) are a real, useful proof of the "every failed attempt" constraint that the brief's snippet didn't itself assert.

**B.5 Minor — coverage gaps not required by the brief but worth noting:**
- No test exercises the exact-boundary length (`s.len() == MAX_ERROR_BYTES`) or the "first char alone exceeds bound" case — both proven safe by code inspection (B.1), not by a test.

input.message:
Task 3 review: spec ✅, but task quality needs work. One **Important** finding. Fix round 1 of 5.

Confirm `git branch --show-current` is the SMA-469 feature branch before touching anything.

---

**Finding (Important) — `truncate_error_bounds_a_long_string_by_bytes_on_a_char_boundary` cannot distinguish the correct implementation from the naive one it exists to guard against.**

`"😀".repeat(700)` is a uniform **4-byte** character, and `MAX_ERROR_BYTES = 1024 = 4 × 256`. So byte offset 1024 is *always* a valid char boundary for this input, regardless of implementation. Concretely: a regression to

```rust
format!("{}…", &s[..MAX_ERROR_BYTES])
```

would produce a byte-for-byte identical result, would **not** panic, and would pass every assertion in your test — `len <=`, `ends_with('…')`, and `chars().all(|c| c == '😀')`. The test's own inline comment claims "a naive byte slice would have panicked before we got here," and for this data that is simply not true.

Your `truncate_error` implementation is correct — that was verified independently by reasoning about `char_indices`. The defect is in the regression protection, not the behavior.

**The fix:** make the cut point land mid-character. Use a character width that does not evenly divide 1024 — a 3-byte char works, since `1024 mod 3 == 1`. For example `"€".repeat(700)` (`€` is 3 bytes, 2100 bytes total): the correct implementation must cut at offset 1023 (the last boundary `<= 1024`), while `&s[..1024]` would land one byte into a character and **panic**. That is a test that genuinely discriminates.

Assert, at minimum:
- the output is `<= MAX_ERROR_BYTES + '…'.len_utf8()` bytes,
- it ends with the elision marker,
- the retained prefix is composed of whole `€` characters,
- and (the point of the exercise) the retained byte length is 1023, not 1024 — i.e. the implementation gave up a byte rather than splitting a character.

Fix the inline comment to state accurately what the data proves.

**While you are rewriting that test, add the two boundary cases that are currently proven only by inspection:**
- a string whose byte length is exactly `MAX_ERROR_BYTES` — must be returned unchanged, with no elision marker appended;
- a string whose first character alone exceeds the bound (you can assert this against the real bound by constructing the input, not by changing the const) — must not panic.

Keep the existing 4-byte-char test if you like, but it is no longer the discriminating one, so do not leave a comment implying it is.

---

**When done:** re-run the covering tests:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.proto/shims:$HOME/.proto/bin:$PATH"
cd rs && cargo nextest run -p paigasus-iam --lib truncate_error
cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --check
```

Then **mutation-test the new test the way you would a real guard**: temporarily replace `truncate_error`'s body with the naive `format!("{}…", &s[..MAX_ERROR_BYTES])`, confirm the new test fails (it should panic), then restore the real implementation and confirm green again. Report both observations — that is the evidence that the test now discriminates.

Append a fix report to the same file (`.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-03-sma-469-outbox-retention-dlq/task-3-report.md`) covering what you changed, the covering tests, the exact commands, their output, and the mutation-test result. Commit with a conventional lowercase subject.

Then return only: STATUS, COMMITS, TESTS (one line), CONCERNS.

Re-review: the primary finding is **ADDRESSED** — the `€` test genuinely discriminates, the byte arithmetic was independently recomputed and confirmed, the exact-boundary test is properly strict, and production code was correctly left untouched. Good work, and the two-direction mutation test was the right evidence.

One new issue that the fix diff itself introduced. Fix round 2 of 5.

---

**`truncate_error_does_not_panic_when_the_first_character_alone_exceeds_the_bound` reintroduces the exact flaw we just fixed, and its comment is wrong.**

It uses `U+0301` (COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT), which is **2 bytes**. `1024 mod 2 == 0`, so byte offset 1024 *is* a valid char boundary for that input — exactly like the `😀` case. Consequences:

- A naive `&s[..1024]` slice would pass this test too. It discriminates nothing.
- The inline comment says "it must still find a real char boundary partway through," which is factually false for this data: the cut lands exactly at 1024, giving up zero bytes.
- It asserts only the bound and the elision marker, with no `prefix.len()` check — so it is silently weaker than its neighbours.

**First, my error, which you should know before fixing:** the case I asked for is **not constructible**. The widest UTF-8 character is 4 bytes, and `MAX_ERROR_BYTES` is 1024, so "a string whose first character alone exceeds the bound" cannot exist unless the const changes. Your instinct to approximate it with a run of combining marks was reasonable; the approximation just landed on a width that reintroduced the flaw. Do not try to salvage the original framing.

**Pick whichever of these you judge better and say why in your report:**

(a) **Delete the test.** The scenario is unconstructible, the `unwrap_or(0)` fallback it was meant to reach is provably unreachable given the early-return guard (as your own Task 3 report already established), and the `€` test covers the real discriminating case. A test that tests nothing is worse than no test.

(b) **Keep it, honestly relabelled.** Rename it to say what it actually covers — a long run of narrow multi-byte characters — switch it to a 3-byte character so the cut is genuinely mid-character, add the `prefix.len()` assertion that makes it discriminate, and rewrite the comment to state only what the data proves.

I lean (a): (b) largely duplicates the `€` test. But you have the code in front of you — your call, with reasoning.

Either way, make sure no remaining inline comment in that test module claims a discriminating property its data does not have. That was the whole point of round 1.

---

```bash

cd rs && cargo nextest run -p paigasus-iam --lib truncate_error
cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --check
```
